    "text": "of clinical development.\n\nExpression of apolipoprotein B100\n\nApolipoprotein (apo) B-containing lipoproteins include LDL, very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), and VLDL remnants. Because these lipoproteins may promote atherosclerosis, strategies to prevent expression of apoB are attractive. However, interference with hepatic export of apoB-containing lipoproteins also has the potential to promote hepatic steatosis.\n\nMipomersen is a 20-base, 2\u2032-O-(2-methoxy) ethyl-modified antisense oligonucleotide that targets mRNA encoding apoB100. It reduces circulating levels of all lipoprotein species containing apoB100 in humans. In Phases 2 and 3 clinical trials of mipomersen as monotherapy or added to statins in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), LDL-C reductions of up to 47% were observed (Visseret al,). Because mipomersen does not significantly affect intestinal apoB48 expression, intestinal fat absorption is unaffected and intestinal steatosis is avoided (Crookeet al, ). However, treatment with mipomersen was associated with injection site reactions, flu-like symptoms, and hepatic steatosis with elevated liver transaminases (Visseret al,).\n\nMipomersen is currently approved for the treatment of homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. However, the long-term benefit/risk profile remains to be determined and might be influenced by tolerability or hepatic safety. Other approaches to knockdown apoB100, including small interfering RNAs, are under investigation (Tadin-Strappset al,).\n\nVLDL assembly \u2013 ACAT and MTP\n\nAnother approach to reduce LDL is to prevent hepatic secretion of its precursor lipoprotein, VLDL, by interfering with the lipidation of apoB. Two enzymes involved in this process, acyl-CoA/cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT) and microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), have been targeted.\n\nACAT1 and ACAT2 are expressed in macrophages as well as liver and intestine where they are involved in accumulation of cholesterol ester, foam cells, atherosclerosis, and providing cholesterol ester to secreted VLDL and chylomicrons (Leeet al,; Leonet al,). Surprisingly, clinical trials that used intravascular ultrasound to evaluate non-specific ACAT inhibitors demonstrated that treatment had a neutral to adverse effect on coronary atherosclerosis (Tardifet al,; Nissenet al,). The explanation may be related to toxic effects of increased free cholesterol in macrophages. Selective ACAT2 inhibition might remain a plausible approach to retard atherosclerosis (Ohshiro & Tomoda, ).\n\nMTP transfers neutral lipids to nascent apoB and thereby affects the rate of VLDL and chylomicron synthesis. Loss-of-function mutation of MTP is the cause of abetalipoproteinemia, a condition with defective fat absorption and the absence of circulating apoB-containing lipoproteins. Lomitapide is a small molecule inhibitor of MTP that was shown to lower LDL-C levels by 50% in patients with homozygous FH and has been approved for the use in that condition (Cuchel & Rader,). Although lomitapide is effective in lowering LDL-C, its use is unlikely to extend beyond FH because of a high incidence of gastrointestinal symptoms related to malabsorption of fat and hepatic steatosis related to inhibition of hepatic lipid export (Cuchelet al,).\n\nThyromimetics or tiromes\n\nThyroid hormone exerts tissue-specific effects, with the thyroid hormone receptor \u03b21 isoform (TR \u03b21) predominating in liver and involved in cholesterol metabolism (Gullberget al,). TR \u03b21 activation depletes intracellular cholesterol concentration, leading to increased expression of the LDL receptor in hepatocytes. Hypolipidemic effects of TR \u03b21 activation are also increased biliary cholesterol excretion through stimulation of cholesterol 7a-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) expression (Linet al,), downregulation of sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP)-1c (Hashimotoet al,), and non-classical signaling pathways (Cordeiroet al,).\n\nThe TR \u03b21 agonists such as eprotirome have been evaluated in clinical trials. On a background of statin treatment, eprotirome lowered LDL-C up to 32%, associated with reductions of apoB, triglycerides, and Lp(a) (Ladensonet al,). Eprotirome was effective in decreasing levels of atherogenic lipoproteins in patients with hypercholesterolemia (Angelinet al,). However, a recent Phase 3 trial was terminated after liver injury was noted in humans and cartilage injury noted in preclinical data with dogs (Sjoukeet al,). Currently, there are no known plans to continue with its development.\n\nPCSK9\n\nbroprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a secreted protein that regulates the hepatic LDL receptor (LDLR), and in turn circulating levels of LDL-C (Akramet al,; Doet al,). When an LDL particle binds to a hepatocyte LDLR in the absence of PCSK9, the LDL/LDLR complex undergoes endocytosis. In the acidic endosome, the LDLR dissociates from LDL and is recycled back to the hepatocyte surface to receive another LDL cargo, while the LDL undergoes lysosomal degradation. When LDL binds to LDLR in the presence of PCSK9, the LDLR does not dissociate from LDL and is instead channeled toward lysosomal degradation. This action reduces LDLR density on the surface of hepatocytes, allowing levels of LDL-C to rise.\n\nGain-of-function mutations in PCSK9 are a cause of familial hypercholesterolemia and premature coronary heart disease, while loss-of-function mutations are associated with lifelong low levels of LDL-C and substantially reduced coronary heart disease risk (Davignonet al, ). Statins increase the expression of PCSK9, an effect that may attenuate the LDL-C lowering produced with these agents (Dubucet al,). Conversely, therapeutic interference with PCSK9 expression or action with small interfering RNA or monoclonal antibody (Frank-Kamenetskyet al,; Diaset al,; Steinet al,) allows greater recycling of LDLR to the hepatocyte surface, resulting in lower LDL-C levels.
